data.name: TheoryStaffSummary
data.value: Music notes live on five lines and four spaces.

data.name: TheoryStaffBody
data.value: The staff is the ladder for written music. Notes can sit on a line or in a space. When a note is too low or too high, we add small ledger lines so the ladder can keep going.

data.name: TheoryTrebleClefSummary
data.value: The treble clef tells us these notes are the higher notes.

data.name: TheoryTrebleClefBody
data.value: The treble clef is also called the G clef. Its curl points to the G line, so that line is sol, or G4. From there the note names climb step by step.

data.name: TheoryTrebleClefCallout
data.value: The highlighted note is sol, also called G4.

data.name: TheoryNoteMapTitle
data.value: Notes from low do to high ti

data.name: TheoryNoteMapSummary
data.value: Read the notes like stair steps from low to high.

data.name: TheoryNoteMapBody
data.value: This first range starts under the staff at low do and climbs to high ti above the staff. Each next line or space moves one step: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti, then do again.

data.name: TheoryNoteMapCallout
data.value: Follow the notes from left to right: every note is one step higher.

data.name: TheorySingleNoteBody
data.value: This page shows {0}. Look at whether the note sits on a line or in a space, and notice if it needs a ledger line.

data.name: TheoryAccidentalsSummary
data.value: A sharp raises a note. A flat lowers a note.

data.name: TheoryAccidentalsBody
data.value: Sharps and flats are accidentals. A sharp moves the note one tiny step higher, and a flat moves it one tiny step lower. The note stays on the same line or space, but the accidental tells you which nearby key to play.

data.name: TheoryBlackKeysSummary
data.value: The same black key can be named as a sharp or a flat.

data.name: TheoryBlackKeysBody
data.value: Look at the black keys between the white keys. The black key above do is do sharp, but it is also re flat. Both names point to the same sound, so either name can be correct depending on the music.

data.name: TheoryBlackKeysCallout
data.value: Each black key shows its sharp name and its flat name.

data.name: TheorySteadyBeatSummary
data.value: The beat is music's steady heartbeat.

data.name: TheorySteadyBeatBody
data.value: A steady beat keeps the same space between every pulse, like footsteps that do not speed up or slow down. Count 1, 2, 3, 4 and clap once on every number. A song can have many different notes while its beat keeps going underneath.

data.name: TheorySteadyBeatCallout
data.value: Say “1, 2, 3, 4” evenly. Each number gets one pulse.

data.name: TheorySteadyBeatPatternLabel
data.value: Four evenly spaced beats numbered 1 to 4

data.name: TheorySoundLengthTitle
data.value: Sounds can be short or long

data.name: TheorySoundLengthSummary
data.value: A sound can stop quickly or keep going across several beats.

data.name: TheorySoundLengthBody
data.value: The beat keeps ticking steadily, but a sound does not always last for the same number of beats. A short sound can stop after one beat. A long sound can stretch across several beats. Keep counting while the sound continues.

data.name: TheorySoundLengthCallout
data.value: The beat tells when to count. The length tells how long the sound keeps going.

data.name: TheoryShortSoundPatternLabel
data.value: A short sound lasting one of four beats

data.name: TheoryLongSoundPatternLabel
data.value: A long sound lasting all four beats

data.name: TheoryBeatDurationsTitle
data.value: Count how long the sound lasts

data.name: TheoryBeatDurationsSummary
data.value: Practice hearing sounds that last for one, two, or four beats.

data.name: TheoryBeatDurationsBody
data.value: Start each sound on beat 1 and keep counting at the same speed. A one-beat sound stops before 2. A two-beat sound continues through 2. A four-beat sound continues through the whole count.

data.name: TheoryBeatDurationsCallout
data.value: Listen with your eyes closed too. Can you hear when each sound stops?

data.name: TheoryBeatDuration1PatternLabel
data.value: One-beat sound shown across a four-beat ruler

data.name: TheoryBeatDuration2PatternLabel
data.value: Two-beat sound shown across a four-beat ruler

data.name: TheoryBeatDuration4PatternLabel
data.value: Four-beat sound shown across a four-beat ruler

data.name: TheoryNoteValuesSummary
data.value: Musicians use different symbols for one-, two-, and four-beat sounds.

data.name: TheoryNoteValuesBody
data.value: You already know these sound lengths. Now give each one its written name and shape. A filled note with a stem lasts one beat, an open note with a stem lasts two beats, and an open note without a stem lasts four beats.

data.name: TheoryNoteValuesCallout
data.value: First count the beats. The symbol is a quick way to remember how long to keep the sound going.

data.name: TheoryNoteValue1SymbolLabel
data.value: Quarter-note symbol: filled note head with a stem

data.name: TheoryNoteValue2SymbolLabel
data.value: Half-note symbol: open note head with a stem

data.name: TheoryNoteValue4SymbolLabel
data.value: Whole-note symbol: open note head without a stem

data.name: TheoryRestsTitle
data.value: The beat keeps going through silence

data.name: TheoryRestsSummary
data.value: A quiet beat is intentional—it is called a rest.

data.name: TheoryRestsBody
data.value: Music needs quiet moments as well as sounds. During a rest, do not play, but keep feeling and counting the steady beat. In this pattern you hear a sound on beats 1 and 3, while beats 2 and 4 stay quiet.

data.name: TheoryRestsCallout
data.value: A rest is not a lost beat. Count it silently so the next sound starts in the right place.

data.name: TheoryRestPatternLabel
data.value: Four-beat pattern: sound on one, rest on two, sound on three, rest on four
